#4063. Gallery: Hollow Knight & Silksong's Switch 2 Physicals Are A Delight For Map Fans

Fangamer announced earlier this year that it had two swanky new Switch 2 physical releases in the works for both Hollow Knight and Silksong, each complete with a couple of bonus goodies inside the box.

With the release date finally upon us, the good folks over at Fangamer have sent us a copy of each, and let it be known, they are both really rather sexy.

Both boxes boast wrap-around cover art (for some particularly detailed spines) and reversible sleeves so you can opt for a design without all of the Switch 2 T&C text down at the bottom.

All of the DLC for the first game is included on the cart, too, and while Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion obviously isn't on there at the moment (we're still waiting for a firm release date on that one), it will come as a free download to all those with a copy when it eventually drops.

Inside, both copies contain some bonus booklet goodies, too. Each has its own instruction booklet, containing introductions for everything from both the Knight and Hornet's movesets and upgrade abilities, to points of interest in the world. Gosh, we didn't realise how much we had missed physical manuals.

A physical copy of each game's map is included in the box as well, which folds up into a little wax-stamped envelope — a very neat touch, if we've ever seen one. This gives you a detailed rundown of each location for both games, and could prove as a valuable route tracker for those still trying to uncover Hallownest/Pharloom's secrets.

Both the Hollow Knight and Silksong Switch 2 physicals are now available on the Fangamer website.

#4062. GTA 6 Will Be Playable On Xbox One Through Xbox Cloud Gaming

Rockstar also confirms GTA 6 will run at 30FPS

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 4:03pm]: According to The Verge's Tom Warren, he believes GTA 6 will only be playable on Xbox Cloud Gaming on consoles, with PC and mobile excluded. Xbox Wire recently posted the three ways to play GTA 6 on Xbox. We've updated the article to reflect this.

Original Story: Buying current-gen Xbox hardware isn't cheap these days, and with GTA 6 is now confirmed to be running 30FPS on Xbox Series X|S, what chance would an Xbox One have of running the game, even if it had launched for previous generation tech?

Well, thanks to Rockstar's pre-load notes, we now know GTA 6 will be playable on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming at Xbox Series S graphics settings. This means those of you who can't upgrade to Xbox Series can still play GTA 6 on November 18th November 19th!

"The game will also be available via XBOX Cloud Gaming on XBOX Series X|S and XBOX One consoles, utilizing XBOX Series S graphics settings. And as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay. GTAVI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and XBOX."

You'll of course be at the mercy of Xbox's fresh Cloud Gaming time caps, limiting how long you can stream games depending on your Xbox Game Pass subscription. You can purchase additional time beyond your allotted amount, and if you're still stuck on Xbox One, topping up your cloud gaming hours could work out cheaper than buying an Xbox Series console. A free ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming is also currently in testing.

However, there may be a catch. According to Tom Warren, it appears that playing GTA 6 via Xbox Cloud Gaming will be restricted to Xbox consoles. If you were planning on streaming the game on PC or mobile, you may need to think again.

"I also incorrectly assumed it would be like every other Xbox Cloud Gaming title and support phone, PC, web, and TV streaming too. GTA 6 is unlike any other game, so clearly an exception has been made here to restrict to just Xbox consoles"

In a recent Xbox Wire post, Microsoft adds weight to Warren's claims, stating the three ways you can play GTA 6 on Xbox:

But back to Rockstar's notes, the Scotland-based dev did indeed confirm that both Xbox and PlayStation devices will target 30FPS whilst pushing the hardware "to their absolute limits" to play GTA 6. My advice would be to give your Xbox a good clean before release. You don't want your console overheating just when the game finally comes out!

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

Pre-loading GTA 6 is live now, even if you don't officially own the game yet. If you'd like to know how, then be sure to check out our preload guide featured at the bottom of this article.

EVE Online is about to have a big week, with the introduction of paid, 24/7 alpha access to companion FPS Vanguard, as well as a new expansion for the OG MMO, Fractured Skies. Both are launching tomorrow, November 10.

That expansion is bringing a bunch of new features⁠—updated HUD, new ships, and further tweaks to the new player experience added over the summer⁠—but when I spoke with EVE design director Greg Hennessey, he was most excited about coming changes to lowsec PvP, and what they'll offer both new and experienced players.

EVE is most famous for the big intrigues and betrayals of nullsec space, but Hennessey estimated that participants in the more structured, constant lowsec conflicts "are actually probably our strongest PVP players in general.

"Our nullsec players are the ones who want to plot for three years and go have a billion dollar war for a year. [Lowsec] players every day are like, let's go out and brawl. Let's just go lose some ships, boys. Let's get out there."

Hennessey characterized Fractured Skies as the "second in a trilogy of expansions" overhauling faction conflict in lowsec. The summer expansion, Cradle of War, added ongoing Military Campaigns players could pitch in with to affect an ongoing story. Fractured Skies will introduce a recurring climax to factional PvP, with the first such Conquest scheduled for February.

"You pick a faction, and for a season, you'll face off against another faction across that season," explained Hennessey. "You will fight to earn points, and all of that drives towards a scheduled final battle. We also know that when people think about EVE Online, they think about big battles in space, but they can be really hard to get into.

"When you start playing, you're like, how do I get into one? When do I show up? And that's kinda 3,000 hours in the end game. But every 10 weeks or so, you're gonna know: I can roll up with whatever I have and go shoot some structures and have a big fight."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

So new players potentially get a smoother introduction to big fleet battles and ongoing participation in a conflict. As for old hands, Hennessey reckons that Conquests will introduce clear resolution and achievement to the constant churn of faction-based struggle.

"What we're saying is: You can win, and you will be recognized for this victory, and that will be recorded in history," he explained. "You'll be remembered for the [theoretical] five-year-long streak of Amar victories that happened. So we're giving them a sense of permanence, a sense of victory, and a sense of accomplishment that I think they felt has been lacking in their actual work or gameplay."

Hennessey also pointed out that Conquests won't exist in a vacuum: They'll impact resource and ship pricing in EVE's emergent economy, while outside forces will be able to influence Conquests in turn. Success in ongoing seasonal events will confer bonuses in the final blowout, but Hennessey pointed out that the underdog could always hire external help to make up the difference. And there's always the possibility someone intervenes and sows chaos just 'cos.

As for the final part of this trilogy of expansions, Hennessey was mum on details, but indicated that there would be a continued emphasis on getting new players to the cool parts of EVE without having to log 3,000 hours of playtime first. In the meantime, Fractured Skies will launch tomorrow through Steam, Epic, and EVE Online's own client.

#4059. GTA 6 PS5 Pro Features Revealed, 30fps Target on Both Consoles

Improved clarity and ray traced shadows on PS5 Pro

Rockstar Games has today revealed what sort of benefits playing GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro will provide.

No matter whether you play on a base PS5 or a PS5 Pro, though, the game will target 30 frames-per-second, a new post on the developer's website confirms:

Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants.

The improvements are slim on PS5 Pro; the article mentions "improved clarity" thanks to PSSR, and there'll be ray traced shadows that are only available on the upgraded console.

There is no 60fps mode, or even a 40fps mode for GTA 6. This also applies to the Xbox Series X|S versions.

Guide GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

The blog post then talks up the game's use of the PS5 DualSense controller, making use of haptic feedback, far better audio, and improved load times. It concludes by calling PS5 the best place to play GTA 6.

As of today, the game is available to preload worldwide on PS5 ahead of the full 19th November launch. Please refer to our GTA 6 Release Times and Preload guide for more information. How do you feel about there being no 40fps or 60fps performance modes in GTA 6? Let us know in the comments below.

@sanderson72 I used to be able to tolerate 30fps, until near the end of last gen.

Then I started getting headaches and feeling sick playing most games - I didn't know what was causing it. It started and got much worse very quickly - only over a period of about 6 months. It completely ruins any chance I have of enjoying a game that is not close to locked 60fps, as it takes hold immediately at 30 or 40fps (and within about 10mins if we are talking about drops at 60fps).

Instead of quitting gaming back then, which I nearly did, I worked out that it was framerate related - something made more difficult by the fact that I knew very little about framerates back then. Now, I can tell if I can tolerate a game by looking at a representative framerate analysis.

I have since spoken to quite a number of people who have experienced similar. I have also helped out a few who, similar to me back then, didn't know what was causing it. 1 in particular was a casual gamer, who happened to mention to me they had started to get headaches playing games. They knew nothing about graphics/performance modes.

Newer TVs seem to make a big difference, but this was not the case for me as I was using a TV I bought in 2016. It seems to be something that can happen to anyone, anytime, but with newer TV tech, and more normalising of 60fps, it seems to be much more common these days.

#4058. Xbox Vs. PS5: GTA 6 Specs Revealed, And These Are The Biggest Differences

"Pushing both platforms to their absolute limits"

Rockstar Games has today lifted the lid on a bunch of specs for both the Xbox and PS5 versions of GTA 6, revealing some of the biggest differences (and similarities) between playing the game on each platform.

The most notable bit of information is that every single console runs the game at 30FPS. Regardless of whether you're playing on Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, PS5 or even PS5 Pro, the max you're getting is 30 frames per-second.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

There will obviously be resolution differences between each platform, but Rockstar has yet to reveal these details. Expect the Series S to fare the worst, the PS5 Pro to fare the best, and the Series X and PS5 to be pretty much equal.

Rockstar does say that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5 though (and let's not forget that Sony appears to have a marketing deal in place with Rockstar Games for this release), highlighting the differences between the PS5 and Xbox versions as being "high-fidelity haptic feedback" for the PS5 DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio rendering, and bizarrely, improved load times. That last one is surely just a minimal advantage at best!

Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 includes high-fidelity haptic feedback fully integrated across the game on DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial audio rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D Audio, and improved load times, making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

Beyond that, the PS5 Pro version will benefit from improved clarity via PSSR along with ray-traced shadows.

However, the Xbox version has one massive benefit in the form of Xbox Cloud Gaming. It seems Xbox will be the only platform offering cloud streaming for GTA 6 at launch, making it an exclusive of sorts - at least for now. The bizarre bit is that it only appears to be for consoles, rather than other devices like PCs and mobiles.

The Xbox and PS5 versions will also support Remote Play (allowing you to cast your game to another device from your console). Nothing has been said about Quick Resume yet on Xbox, but we assume it'll be supported as well.

Ultimately, GTA 6 is bound to run great regardless of whether you buy it on Xbox or PlayStation, and the "plays best on PS5" differences mentioned by Rockstar Games appear to be minor advantages rather than major ones.

We can't wait for footage to start appearing online next week — especially for the Xbox Series S version — and here's hoping it's going to live up to the ridiculous hype that's been fueling the past decade. Not long to wait at all now!

#4057. Talking Point: With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

"The line must be drawn here! This far, no further!"

Please forgive the Captain Picard First Contact quote (it's been a couple of weeks since Patrick Stewart's death and only now can I mention his most famous character without welling up) - I promise it's relevant as an illustration of an admirable, principled stance.

In the Borg, good ol' Jean-Luc had a well-defined enemy to engage, with the threat of humanity's assimilation providing a pretty clear line between good and bad. There are larger philosophical questions about the hive mind and our aversion to Star Trek's cube-riding automatons, but for the purposes of this article, let's assume we're all in agreement: Borg=baaad.

Back in the real world, though, that line between right and wrong often isn't so easy to define. Today there'll be a lot of commentators in the video game space, players and developers alike, longing for a better understanding of another encroaching, all-consuming entity.

House House's belated disclosure that LLMs were used during the development of indie hit Big Walk pours fuel on an already raging debate and brings questions over permissible AI use in game dev right back into the discourse - specifically the differences between generative AI for player-facing audio-visual assets and writing versus coding and other less obvious uses.

News Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

This latest flashpoint followed a statement released by a subset of IGF Award jurors explaining why they won't be voting for games developed using any form of generative AI.

Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — which swept The Game Awards with nine wins from 13 nominations — raised similar questions after the Indie Game Awards disqualified Sandfall Interactive's game upon discovering AI had been used in the development pipeline.

I've voiced my distaste for GenAI, and it remains a massive no-no - professionally and personally. I'm fortunate to not have corporate overlords mandating its use around these parts, which certainly isn't the case for some other outlets, nor for many creatives in the gaming space. The gulf in quality between the human-written word and generated bilge is still enormous and easily identifiable, and for now, the same is broadly true of GenAI visual artwork, too.

What this Big Walk situation highlights, however, is how difficult it can be to discern in other places, and the increasing pull it has on even the most principled developers.

Talking Point Does It Bother You That Big Games Companies Are Using GenAI?

The phrase gets bandied around a lot, but it's fair to call Big Walk a proper 'critical darling'. It garnered "Universal Acclaim" back in August, with an impressive 91 Metascore. Alex gave it a "Great" 8/10 after reviewing the Switch 2 version for us - technical hiccups took the shine off it for him, but he still loved the co-op experience. And by September it was already Nile's GOTY.

As someone who didn't play Big Walk at launch, its place in my GOTY-catch-up priorities may have shifted, but wherever you land on the GenAI spectrum, the consensus among critics and players is as unanimous as it gets: Big Walk is an excellent video game.

There are many issues to consider — not least where AI use crosses from tool to theft — but an important one relates to how this game in particular has had a profound effect on many players. Rejecting something flagged as 'suspicious' on principle is easy, especially with so many brilliant games releasing each week. But something you've played already and internalised and loved? From a dev team you respect?

For some, this revelation will feel like when a beloved artist/actor/writer/musician is revealed to be problematic, but we're not talking about illegal behaviour or allegations here.

If House House's statement is to be taken at face value, the team used a chatbot to find a solution to a coding issue with Unity, the third-party engine the game is built on. People online with real chops have already investigated the specifics of House House's single example:

took me 3 hours but I figured out the “URP culling shadowcasters behind the camera” issue House House cites in their disclosure. This culls immediately when the object is off-camera, but modifying the culling params with a custom frustrum is straightforward

this needs cleaning up but is basically the gist

This was a terrible use of 3 hours, but I know just a bit more about how to do something cool. I’m sympathetic to them wanting to ship something good but AI rots your damn brain

That's the one example the devs offer in their statement, and the language around further usage feels vague. The impression it gives is of a team searching for a solution to a specific problem using common tools, as opposed to vibe-coding huge swathes of the game.

Now, I've never programmed anything in my life, but I can appreciate that efficient code must be an art in itself. Is it any less of an art because that code is invisible to players? Then again, to me, generating great chunks of game code feels very different from using an LLM to squash a bug or find a solution when third-party documentation fails. Is one usage as 'bad' as the other, or is this slippery slope, gateway-drug territory?

(Perhaps if any programmers are reading, they'd like to share thoughts in the comments - as the headline says, this is very much a talking point and I'm keen to explore with as much nuance as the internet will permit.)

My point is that seeing exactly where to draw that line is increasingly difficult when AI tools of all types become ubiquitous. A blanket rejection of anything inevitably now means excluding not just an increasing number of games, but also artistically significant, important ones.

And with executives like former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser advocating the use of AI for indie teams to improve workflow, it's also easy to understand how a developer might turn to the tech. The whole topic is getting greyer by the day, much to the pleasure of evangelists, I'm sure.

Like it or not, this situation forces AI sceptics to reconcile their positive feelings for the game. House House estimates "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" has any trace of generative AI, but to paraphrase a certain Starfleet captain again, "How much does it take before it becomes wrong, hmm?" That is the question.

For some players who simply don't care, it's a non-issue. Some may reluctantly cut the game from their lives and GOTY lists. I suspect that others, though, disappointed or otherwise, will start reconsidering where they personally draw the AI line.

And if House House hadn't disclosed this, would anyone have ever known? I'd guess not. And if a celebrated indie team turned to AI as a problem-solver, how many other devs aren't disclosing similar usage? And how many sure-as-hell won't do so after this?

Lots of questions, no clear answers, just murk. How unsatisfying. I've heard 'ends-justify-means' sentiments online — 'hey, if the game is good, does it matter?' — which feel unsavoury given the documented, quantifiable damage AI is doing to the games industry and the wider world. It's that damage which has IGF jurors abstaining from voting for Big Walk this year: an understandable, admirable stance.

Which leads us to one final question: What would Captain Picard do?

Naturally, he'd call everyone into the Observation Lounge for a big old meeting in a calm, civilised manner, that's what. Conference.

Let us know below if this revelation changes your relationship with the game or where you draw the line when it comes to generative AI in its various forms.

I'm anti-AI in almost all facets of life, but I also have always said that no absolute is ever going to be proper (including that one). I see this particular instance as a very slippery slope. As for the inevitability of AI's spread in game development, I take the approach that I take with student work; it's fine to use as a tool to check for mistakes, but nothing you submit should ever be made in any capacity with AI. Uploading a paper to ChatGPT and saying "List every grammatical error" so that you can fix things your own proofreading missed or that violated grammatical conventions you didn't know? Acceptable. Going to ChatGPT and saying "Write a five page essay on the causes and effects of the Mexican-American War"? Unacceptable. Feeding a game into an AI model and saying "Look for game-breaking bugs"? Acceptable. Using code made by gen AI? Unacceptable.

And of course, none of that addresses the environmental degradation caused by AI, the absolute havoc it's caused in the electronics market, and the brownouts resulting from the massive power drain of data centers. When you factor in those considerations, I'm solidly on team "no AI ever."

I’m not a game dev but a software engineer with over 15 years of end-to-end more than just full stack software development experience who helped build up 2 successful startups with my own hand written code, no matter the coding language, backend, front end, infrastructure as code.

I’ve started to increasingly use AI because in today’s world it would burn you out to do anything without AI with all the pressure coming from needing to survive as a business.

My own rule is simply to use AI only to the capacity that ensures you have full control and AI doesn’t take over, and not in a way that replaces Human Resources but improves efficiency. In art this is difficult to achieve, but for coding it is simple.

1) If it’s some quick one-time tedious type of work (e.g. migrating to a new system), AI can be immensely helpful, you only need to review the end-result/output. I find the use of AI okay if you are capable of ensuring quality output and review it.

I had AI write scripts to do several types of migration work where it would take me weeks to learn all the tiny bits and unknowns, then write all the code. I used to do it all by hand and it is thankless work where you learn a lot of things you will never apply again in your life. Perfect scenario for AI to just do it. It can research everything needed and think of unknowns you couldn’t think of. Once the work is done, throw the scripts away because migration is done. Weeks of work reduced to a mere few hours. Instead I can focus on more fun parts of my job.

2) if its production level code that impacts user experience, I feel you should only use AI for assistance to improve and not to build. You need full control. We had an instance in the company somebody wrote the entire microservice via AI in a way he was incapable of debugging without AI. One part of it I had to rewrite completely by hand to fix it. They had no clue what they were doing and it could have been a disaster.

Unfortunately, I personally have come across too many lazy developers that make me prefer AI written code over their code, because AI simply codes better, more structured, can follow design patterns properly.

If you are unable to clearly envision the expected logic you intend to write, the expected design patterns used, don’t use AI. Learn first.

This brings me to 3) using AI to improve your skills is an extremely powerful tool. I told a friend to have AI teach him design patterns since I have no time for doing that, but he can always cross check with me. He has never improved so fast in his own hand-written creations before AI.

— Now I’ve tried using AI in various ways for coding and one thing for sure is that you need to be extremely good in giving boundaries and directions. Basically the correct “prompt”, and you can only do that if you have enough experience and skills yourself to control AI in that way. And you can never get there if you just let AI do all the work. It makes a lot of mistakes.

Now if I had to not worry about money, I would use AI far less and only for code reviews or learning, basically jsut as “feedback”, not a producer. But that’s not something I can afford, especially in a world where all employers now expect you to use AI to improve cost-efficiency.

Maybe not a common take, or a popular one, but I'm not a developer, yet I've been able to do amazing things with AI that I never could have without it. I have always had ideas and never been able to do anything with them because I lack the skill to code, and the time/desire to learn.

Since picking up Claude Code less than a year ago I've made several small games for myself that were terrible and I abandoned, but I've also been able to make some great stuff:

All of these projects are open source, on my github, and I will never charge for them, so I have the luxury of saying if you don't like it, don't use it. But I can sympathize with people who CAN code and are being forced to work faster not smarter on commercial projects, or losing their jobs altogether because 1 developer can do the work of 3, with the quality of none.

At work I've been able to (with my CEO's blessing) teach an AI agent how to fix 80% of the issues we see regularly to the point where over half of my daily work is done now with fully deterministic code, written by an AI agent, and the rest is triaged and investigated before I ever see it. Our time to resolution has gone down, and customer satisfaction has gone up, and we still send every communication by hand. None of the code is user facing, and none is supported by our dev team, so it's only to benefit our support staff.

I'm absolutely against using AI to replace people, whether it's in development, design, art, writing, communication, or anywhere else, but I'm a huge proponent of using it to enable your team to hand-off the time consuming, repetitive tasks to agents and focus on the things that the love about their job instead.

I'm very anti AI. I also turn my TV against the wall in case it steals my soul.

@Slowdive I think your blanket statement is at odds with the nuance the article is calling for.

"Do you use Google search? Then you are BAD. EVIL. NO GOOD."

One of the most common defenses of AI is that it's just a tool. This is, technically, true.

A hammer is also a tool. You can use a hammer to make a beautiful birdhouse. You can use it to make an ugly birdhouse. Or you can use it to bash in the brains of someone who criticized your birdhouse.

The difference is that there are already well established rules/laws in place about ethical hammer usage. With AI, we're really only getting started, and it's probably going to take a long time to figure out all the nuances, especially with a technology that will only continue to evolve.

I am also aware that there are environmental concerns, but I don't know enough to comment.

@OrangeSoda I mean, those laws haven't stopped hammers from being used wronfully.

Also, any actual illegal use of AI has already had people prosecuted. People generating pics that harm others have been jailed.

Of course when it's about copyright and whatever about protecting IPs, where it's a more grey issue about what is or isn't fair use, no one has faced actual consequences.

Tomorrow, November 10, EVE Online is releasing a new expansion, Fractured Skies, and companion FPS EVE Vanguard is going into something Fenris Creations is calling a 24/7 alpha. Formal early access on Steam is coming late next year, but you can buy the game and play it through EVE's own client⁠—and it won't go away like prior playtests.

Tomorrow will also see Vanguard start to fulfill its promise as a linked game to EVE Online⁠—completing contracts in the multiplayer FPS will create military campaign opportunities players can find and act on in EVE—marking the return of a dream Fenris (formerly CCP Games) has pursued since the ill-fated PS3 shooter, Dust 514. I sat down with Vanguard game director Scott Davis and EVE design director Greg Hennessey to talk about what's coming tomorrow and further down the line.

From a pure gameplay perspective, Davis told me that NPC AI and new player onboarding are the biggest improvements in Vanguard since its last playtest. The NPC enemies inhabiting Vanguard's levels just weren't challenging enough, and while it's easy to make them better shots, the problem was more one of tactical depth.

"We had a lot of people bounce off the game pretty hard in July," Davis said of the other issue, Vanguard's new player experience. "I think we'd accidentally created the most hardcore extraction game of all time, because we had some awkward intricacies to how weapon upgrading and healing worked in the game." There will be more direct tutorializing to address this in tomorrow's Alpha, and a lot of thought has also gone into how Vanguard introduces its modes to players.

New players will be introduced through a full co-op/PvE mode, which will then unlock the PvEvP from the last playtest. The final mode sounds the most exciting and unique, though: Davis described it as a PvP-first "3v3v3 procedurally generated labyrinth, where you just go in and only one team can get out alive."

That sounds sick, and reminds me a bit of Marathon's Cryo Archive pinnacle activity. I'm encouraged by the variety of playstyle options Vanguard is offering: Marathon seems to have ultimately been sunk by its pure focus on hardcore PvP, while Vanguard might have an advantage attracting and holding a healthy playerbase with such varied modes.

The back of the box pitch for Vanguard is that what happens in the FPS will impact EVE Online's one-of-a-kind digital economy, and vice versa. I keep saying it's like the jocks (FPS guys) teaming up with the nerds (spreadsheet EVE guys), and people generally smile politely when I do.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The 24/7 alpha is coming with a first version of that interoperability, with mission completion unlocking mining and combat activities in EVE Online. The next big step in this connection is planned for the second quarter of 2027. At that point, Fenris plans for Vanguard players to be able to declare allegiance with one of the four main empires in EVE, then have their mission progress contribute to the Military Campaign and Conquest systems introduced in EVE's latest two expansions.

Davis sees the empire allegiance system as a major step by Vanguard toward EVE's style of emergent player behavior. One thing he's looking forward to: Vanguard players adopting faction heraldry on their characters, and the sorts of Arc Raiders moments it may foment out in the wild. Maybe you hold fire on a stranger in PvEvP mode because you recognize you're both aligned with the same faction. Alternately, maybe you go out of your way to hunt down a player because they're aligned with an opposing empire.

I was curious if linking the two games had presented any technical difficulties, but both Davis and Hennessey told me it's been surprisingly smooth sailing. "We've sent up many flares ourselves before, but we haven't really had many messages back," Davis told me. "And I wouldn't call it a technical hurdle, because everyone's been working really hard and they know how to do it. But I think that there will be a champagne popping moment of getting those first messages back from EVE Online."

Hennessey, meanwhile, said it's less an issue of connecting the two games. Rather, he pointed out that making a game is hard, making two is twice as hard, and that these two games of very different genres have to align with and compliment each other.

But I hope it pays off, because this vision of two, nested live games changing and influencing each other in real time is like nothing else out there. If it speaks to you, you can wishlist EVE Vanguard on Steam or check out its paid alpha tomorrow through the EVE launcher.

#4055. Xbox CEO Issues Statement On GTA 6 And New '10-Year Partnership' With Its Publisher

The game is also now the most pre-ordered Microsoft Store title ever

We're getting a whole ton of GTA 6 details coming out today, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has taken to social media to issue a statement about the game's pre-orders, as well as a new 10-year partnership with its publisher Take-Two.

Sharma didn't share any specific details about the partnership in her post, but we did cover the deal at the beginning of October, which allows Take-Two to develop and sell Xbox-compatible products across all Xbox devices. The Xbox boss did also highlight that GTA 6 has now set a record for the most pre-orders of any Microsoft Store / Xbox Store game in history.

It's no surprise that the most anticipated game of all time is picking up its fair share of pre-orders ahead of launch. The numbers were looking good as early as August, when Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick described GTA 6's pre-orders as "unprecedented and astonishing".

Of course, Zelnick wasn't talking solely about Xbox's pre-order total, but it's great to see Sharma commenting on Microsoft's numbers specifically.

Beyond handling Rockstar's GTA and Red Dead Redemption IPs, Take-Two Interactive also manages 2K and Zynga titles. If Sharma intends to entertain more than a billion players every day, striking up a cloud streaming deal with Take-Two is a great place to start.

The latest Zelda game is "off to a great start," says Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo says The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is "off to a great start" and the 40th Anniversary Edition Switch 2 console has also been "very positive," heading off speculation from an investor that price hikes may be hurting momentum.

Taking questions as part of its latest financial briefing, Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa is pressed on how well the Switch 2 is selling its wares after the console's price jumped to $500 earlier this year. Investors reckon things are slowing down, and they don't like that. As such, one asks the Nintendo suits whether they think current financial goals will still be met.

The short answer is absolutely; just look at how well Zelda's Ocarina of Time remake and 40th-anniversary console are doing.

"Adoption has progressed smoothly over the roughly one and a half years since Nintendo Switch 2 launched last June, and the installed base now exceeds 25 million units," Furukawa says. "At the end of last year's holiday season, we explained that there were regional differences in how well our expectations were met. But the March release of Pokemon Pokopia acted as a driver of global hardware sales, and we entered the new fiscal year with good momentum."

Furukawa continues by saying that, while the Switch 2 did indeed increase in price, the impact hasn't been too great because most people were given plenty of notice and have had plenty of hardware and software bundles to compensate for it.

That takes us to today, where Nintendo is seemingly riding high thanks to all things Zelda. Furukawa says the special version of the Switch 2 designed to celebrate Zelda's 40th anniversary has been "very positive" for the company and has "contributed to strong sales in various regions." Meanwhile, while it's too early to delve too far into the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake numbers, Furukawa says it's "off to a great start," and that Nintendo is in "good shape for the coming holiday season," too.

"Holiday season sales significantly impact the number of units shipped annually for our dedicated video game platform business," he says. "Given the hardware price revisions, we think the sales trends over the next several weeks will be key to achieving our sales guidance."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

While no official numbers are given, there are signs that, yeah, those Zelda products are shifting units. As per Circana, the Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 drove record sales for Nintendo in the US. In fact, it was only last month that a Nintendo exec said those at the house of Mario "underestimated" how well it would sell. Stock has been an issue, though a welcome one.

We have less to go on with the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. That said, analyst firms say the N64 throwback is the largest physical launch in the UK so far this year. With the festive period coming up, I can see why Nintendo isn't sweating this one too hard right now.

Nintendo "bearing" Switch 2 manufacturing costs to avoid price hikes – but that may have to change if "we cannot absorb the costs through our own efforts."

#4053. Unknown 9 Dev Being Shut Down Two Years After Disaster PS5 Launch

Do you remember Unknown 9: Awakening? Published by Bandai Namco, the story-driven stealth-action title had a fairly hard marketing push ahead of its release back in October 2024 — but it was labelled a "failure" just months after its launch.

It was a commercial disaster, selling way below expectations, and developer Reflector Entertainment was subsequently hit with layoffs, before revealing that it would be put to work on an existing Bandai Namco property.

Bandai Namco itself had acquired the Canadian studio in 2020. We don't know how much the deal was worth, but it's now been confirmed that the publisher ate an "extraordinary" 3.5 billion yen loss on Unknown 9. That's approximately $22 million / £16 million / €21 million.

That's according to Bandai Namco's own press release, which also confirms Reflector Entertainment's closure.

"After comprehensively considering future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation, the Company has decided to discontinue Reflector’s business, dissolve and liquidate it," the company writes.

It's a brutal end for a team that has seemingly been in limbo since launching Unknown 9. Whatever existing property the developer was working on, the project clearly didn't make the cut.

We wish those impacted by the closure all the best for the future.

World of Warcraft: Forever made some changes to how dungeons work—rather than getting a bunch of XP from enemies in dungeons, you predominantly get experience points from the quests surrounding them.

Which is made slightly better for the fact that there are just more dungeons overall—so while you can't sit in dungeons until level 60, you can chain between those dungeons with minimal questing, though some questing is still basically mandatory if you care about being efficient.

This has been a point of consternation. Any brief visit over to the r/classicwow subreddit leads to a raft of complaint threads about dungeon XP, though other communities do vary. It should be mentioned that a singular subreddit isn't reflective of the game's entire population, mind—but it is notable how upset the dungeon-loving slice of WoW's playerbase is.

To try and soothe that ache, Blizzard's gone ahead and buffed the XP gain: "At about 11:05 PST today, we deployed a hotfix that increased kill experience in dungeons by 50%, so it feels better to go back in for more runs," writes community manager Kaivax. "Happy dungeon crawling, and good luck with those Deviate Hides!"

That 50% number isn't actually too much, mind—it's a 50% increase to the current value. So let's say you were getting 40 XP from a mob: You're now getting 60.

For the record, I'm a touch on the fence about this one. I do think that the amount of XP from enemies alone was kind of unhealthy for the game. You do want those repeat runs to give a decent batch of experience, not just for folks who would rather spend their time rinsing dungeons with their mates, but also so healers and tanks have a reason to come back to them and to keep the dungeon-delver's population healthy after the launch week rush.

On the other hand, I'm kind of fine with dungeons giving a huge batch of XP up front and then not being the best way to level thereafter. It's ultimately okay if World of Warcraft: Forever is a videogame about questing or exploring the open world.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

But I can see the other side of the coin: The major problem is that Forever's also been pitched as a game about returning to the Azeroth you knew, but with a shinier coat of paint. And for some WoW players, that Azeroth predominantly took place in instanced content with a bunch of their buddies over Teamspeak or Ventrilo. I don't think they're wrong for feeling hard done-by.

If you were to put the balancing in my hands (you shouldn't) I'd say dungeon grinding ought to be just a little behind questing as an XP source, given you get such a massive bump of XP from dungeon quests on your first run. Still worthwhile, but nothing that's going to outpace playing to Forever's strengths.

I just hope this design isn't completely walked back, though, because I think Forever will be a stronger game if it sticks to its guns, even if that's not to everyone's tastes—because games are generally more interesting when they do that.

#4051. 'Generally Favourable' Review Scores For Trio Of Xbox Game Pass Launch Titles

Decent scores for Warhammer Survivors, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, and Football Manager 27

Three games from November's Xbox Game Pass lineup are launching today, and they're already picking up some pretty decent review scores.

Warhammer Survivors, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, and Football Manager 27 Console are available for Ultimate and PC Game Pass members today. It's a pretty busy day for the service, especially if you're interested in playing all three, so we decided to do quick review roundup of them all.

This way you can see what the critics are saying and maybe decide which game you fancy playing first. So, here's what reviews are saying about the three new Xbox Game Pass titles:

"You’ll find yourself smiling as you log dozens and dozens of hours in this installment of Football Manager, which takes a leap forward from last year’s revolutionary release, offering a more polished, streamlined game with even faster processing speeds. The loss of official team name licenses is becoming a serious problem, but once you get past that hurdle, Football Manager 27 offers a well-rounded managerial experience that’s increasingly optimized and satisfying." - Google Translate

"Football Manager 2027 marks a strong return to previous highs, following the stumbles last year, with the standout feature being the impressive and engaging changes to the tactics system, enhanced by greater control and noticeable feedback. Fans of the series should, and will, enjoy it, and it will make a good move forward for those who have been sticking with FM24."

"Football Manager 27 has finally regained its appeal with improved controls and greater tactical depth. Unfortunately, AI glitches and missing features continue to be a nuisance."

"We have not yet returned to the levels of Football Manager 2024: the interface needs to strike a more convincing balance between accessibility and efficiency, while the game engine remains the primary obstacle to the project’s full success. It is difficult to overlook certain player behaviors when the rest of the game encourages an ever-greater focus on tactical preparation."

"Tanuki: Pon's Summer is a charming, nostalgia-filled adventure that captures the magic of childhood summers through BMX exploration, quirky characters, and an impressive variety of mini-games. Its vibrant rural Japanese setting and fantastic soundtrack make every delivery feel like a new discovery. While limited BMX tricks and underdeveloped shrine customization leave room for improvement, Pon's summer adventure is a heartfelt experience that's easy to get lost in."

"This adorable adventure has clearly been made with a lot of care and attention, and that shines through in the engaging cycling gameplay and the endearing characters. Its mini-games do their best to hide the fact that the game's mainly a series of fetch quests, but the love that's gone into making it is contagious."

"Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is the rare cosy game that truly lives up to its premise, balancing both whimsical and snarky humour, alongside gameplay that manages to keep you moving just enough to hide its more shallow mechanics. Combined with a surprisingly generous array of content and impressive presentation, this is a Game Pass launch well worth checking out, even if a few wobbly wheels may disrupt your journey."

"TANUKI: Pon’s Summer is seriously charming, and that goes a long way to papering over some of the issues I had with it. If you loved Pon as much as I did then you'll definitely enjoy your summer with him."

"Warhammer Survivors is as addictive as Vampire Survivors, but has some unique twists that keep the experience interesting. It's also nearly flawless on the Steam Deck."

"All in all, Warhammer Survivors perfectly melds Games Workshop's property with poncle's timeless formula, resulting in another exceptional roguelike experience."

Mini Review Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell

"If you’re looking for the next twist on the Vampire Survivors formula and the idea of a Warhammer spin-off excites you, absolutely do not skip Warhammer Survivors – it’s on virtually every platform, it isn’t demanding on the system and and it’s quite cheap. It’s full or Warhammer goodness from two universes, and it introduces various twists the make the combat more varied and engaging. A slow start and the game being a lot less varied and content-filled than Poncle‘s masterpiece do limit the game’s long-term potential, but Warhammer‘s survivors-like romp is a blast, one that will keep me glued to the screen for quite some time even after this review."

"Considering these examples, Warhammer Survivors is a few days late and dollars short, albeit at a budget price. For those of you who’ve fully rinsed Vampire Survivors… Well, first off, that’s simply an impressive feat; well done. But secondly, here are another 40 heroes to max out, with hundreds of objectives to clear. Consider your bullet heaven buffet fully restocked."

There you have it, folks! Decent scores all around for today's Xbox Game Pass launch titles. Of the three, Football Manager 27 appears to have impressed the most, but only time will tell if that remains the case. Warhammer Survivors is pulling in mixed scores, although there's still a chance its score could climb a smidge.

#4050. Marathon's Fate Hangs in the Balance as Bungie Details Its Game-Saving PvE Update

Bungie has reconfirmed that Marathon's major 'Symbiosis' update will launch on the 8th December. You may recall that it was delayed back in September.

Many believe that this patch will be the troubled shooter's make-or-break moment, as Marathon's player numbers remain concerningly low.

The good news is that Symbiosis looks the part. A new trailer highlights its additions, which include a brand new PvE mode titled Expedition.

The official description reads: "Phase 1 of a new PvE-only mode built around a three-run series. Play solo or with a crew, face new combat and environmental challenges without PvP threats, and use Flash Boosts to shape your build during a run."

Basically, Bungie's hoping that the introduction of a non-competitive option draws in new players — and I suppose that's a logical avenue to go down, given that Marathon's struggled to crack the extraction shooter market.

The update also packs a new team-based 'Deathmatch' mode in its beta form, a new social space called Limbo, and a new Runner Shell (character class) named Bishop. A couple of new weapons are up for grabs, too.

And last but certainly not least, Marathon's going free-to-play for a full week when the Symbiosis update drops. Worth a shot?

Do you still play Marathon? Might you be going back for this big update? Check those corners in the comments section below.

#4049. MSI Maestro 900R PC case review

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close, there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

It's just me in the office today. Normally that's fine. I don't mind the quiet, and I can be as messy as I like without Jacob tutting at me. Today is different. Today that comes with a healthy dose of fear. Fear because I have to lift the MSI Maestro 900R case up onto the test bench desk, and I don't think Paul, the oddball security guard way downstairs at the front desk, will hear me if I scream because my spine has snapped. It's a two person job and I'm very much a one-person team in PC Gamer towers today. I have managed to get it situated on the desk, but I can certainly feel it in my near fifty-year-old back muscles. *Spasm*. And when you need another human on hand every time you want to shift your gaming PC about, I think that says a lot about both this MSI case and who it's aimed at.

In short, I think you need to be someone who has their own staff.

That's partly a dig at its sheer scale—this thing is chomk with a capital CHOMK—but also at the fact only the very wealthy are going to consider this chassis a worthwhile casing for their gaming PC. This is a $700 (£800) PC case and that feels, on one hand, par for the course in these days of hyper-expensive everything, but also faintly anachronistic.

As always with the case reviewing process, I built a new PC inside it, and it only felt right to be doing so with high-end gear. So, I picked from the review kit that was in the cupboard: a MSI Godlike X with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D seemed appropriate, along with some 64 GB of G.Skill ULL memory and an RTX 5090. And that's when this whole endeavour started to feel like something from a bygone age.

Before, when I'd do a high-end build, it felt exciting in a way that was both special—because I could never spend out on such premium parts myself—but also still kind of achievable, too, because the money wasn't so far beyond the realms of decency that you couldn't imagine someone normal pushing their budget a little far to get this sort of kit. But looking at the parts going into this, it's around $12,000 worth of kit at least. And that feels well beyond a normal PC gamer and into faintly distasteful territory.

But, in all honesty, I'm not even totally convinced the MSI Maestro 900R really deserves its place in such company. Sure, it's elegant in black and gold trim, but there are odd touches here and there which belie the super premium pricing. The most egregious is something I picked out when I saw a preview case out at Computex this year, and that's the top flair on the case. The metal 'lid' only covers half of the dust filter for the 360 mm cooler I'd mounted to the top, and that filter is just a flimsy plastic one I wouldn't really want on display.

I also question the utility of having the motherboard and GPU's outputs all out of reach in the centre of the case, behind tempered glass shields. There are a ton of Type-A and Type-C USB ports on the front panel, but still it's a lot of effort to get to the I/O panel of your motherboard. And don't get me started on the PSU buried right in the back of the case, with impossible-to-reach switches and plug sockets.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

But there are things I like, too. The wraparound glass does look great, and I loved having so much space to work in when building into the rig. And to have that full central motherboard tray be completely removable was a treat, as well. You essentially have your own little test rig there, so you can make sure everything works before you do the full install. It's neat. As is the final build.

But honestly, this feels more like a chassis you might buy for someone else to build into. Because you're Mr. or Mrs. Moneybags and don't want to get your hands dirty doing manual labour and just want to have a high-end rig to play your games on in something that stands like a glass and gold monolith in the bespoke gaming room of your palace.

✅ You only have a passing knowledge of what's in your bank account: If you watch the pennies this isn't a chassis for you, but if you don't—and you're into the black, glass, and gold aesthetic, and have the space—then maybe it's worth considering.

❌ You need regular access to your mobo's I/O panel: The Maestro 900R hides it all away inside the case, meaning you have to open it up to get at the back of your motherboard.

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

Regular: E-ATX / ATX / Micro-ATX / Mini-ITX

1 x LED Switch Button · 1 x Mic-in / Audio-out · 1 x Power Button · 4 x USB 5Gbps (Type-A) · 4 x USB 10Gbps (Type-C) · 1 x USB 20Gbps (Type-C)

Top: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm · Side: 6 x 120 mm · Bottom: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm

Top: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm · Side: 120 / 240 / 360 mm · Bottom: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm

695 x 379 x 671 mm / 27.36 x 14.92 x 26.42 inches

Net weight: 33 kg / 72.75 lbs · Gross weight: 38 kg / 83.78 lbs

The key things to note are the sheer size of this beast. At well over 30 kilos, this is a massive chassis and when you've built a rig into it, that weight only goes up. It's a two-person job shifting this thing around, as my poor back can attest to.

The other thing is that it is really pleasing to build into. Thanks, in part, to the size of the case and the space you have to work in, but also because of that central motherboard tray. It is effectively a standalone test bench, and makes putting the board itself in place a doddle. It's also rotatable, so you can orient your system inside however you'd like. And because all the external cables need to be routed around from inside to outside anyways, you don't have to worry about where the mobo's I/O is going to go because it'll largely be inaccessible anyways.

To help this you have four 10 Gbps Type-C USB ports on the front of the case, along with a further 20 Gbps Type-C with 60 W power delivery, and four 5 Gbps USB Type-A ports. That does salve some of the pain of not being able to access your motherboard's back panel.

The other useful thing is that it comes with three 160 mm reverse blade fans, so the intakes on the base don't show their ugly side and ruin the high-end aesthetic.

Installation is an absolute joy… until it isn't. That occurs towards the end of the build, but at the start it really is all fun and games. The removable fan tray makes it easy to get your 360 mm radiator in place and the scale of the case means there's always space to work in when you've pulled the tool-free side panels off.

That motherboard tray is excellent, too. I was a big fan of that when I saw it out at Computex, and have been just as impressed now I've used it properly. The issue is that if you want to test out the components you've bought for this build using it as a standalone test bench, you will have to largely break it all down again before you can jam it into the system itself. But that's to be expected, and being able to just get your motherboard, CPU, cooling bracket, SSD, and RAM in place free from even the modest constraints of this massive rig is a real boon.

The installation pain is rear-loaded, however, and once you've got everything inside and wired up internally it then becomes a game of figuring out how the hell you're actually going to attach this thing up to either power or a monitor. There is no real back to this case, with the wraparound tempered glass surrounding the entire plane you mount the motherboard too. That means all the cables, from power, to display, to networking and anything else going into the back of your board, need to be routed out of some grommeted holes on the underside of the case.

It means you'll likely need a longer HDMI or DP cable than you have right now, because it needs to be routed in and around the inside of the case to get to the vertically mounted graphics card, which cuts a lot off its length. And you're unlikely to be sitting this on a desktop given its girth, so it's going to need to stretch from the ground up. Similarly, the power cable for the PSU has to be squeezed into the case, and if you're using a large PSU—such as the MSI MEG Ai1600T brick I've been using—then that doesn't give you a lot of space to attach its fat plug.

But that lack of a busy, cable-heavy backside to the case does really aid the aesthetic. The shroud (which is sadly quite flimsy plastic) that covers the rear of the vertically mounted GPU and the rear of the motherboard hides all the cables that sprout from their outputs as they're fed out the underside of the case, and that gives it a really clean finish. Inside, it looks like there is almost nothing connecting the components, leaving them looking like they're floating around inside. The MSI Godlike X motherboard only helped this by hiding a lot of its power cabling, too.

The angled reverse-bladed fans on the bottom intake are slightly angled, which allows you to see them in all their RGB LED glory, but that, coupled with the angling of the top radiator mount, makes it feel even bigger inside. I really like the full wraparound tempered glass, too. It really gives it a showpiece aesthetic, which I can see being used at a bunch of PC trade show booths in the future.

What slightly ruins that aesthetic, however, is the exposed plastic dust cover on the top of the case. The metal cover, which slots on without screws, only partially covers the things, leaving it open to be eyeballed. And it's not a great look. Likewise, the plastic shroud covering the cables inside looks and feels flimsy. It's the same with the power and LED buttons on the front panel. They look like they could have come from any $50 chassis, as does the lightbar on the rear side of the case's top.

It is not the most expensive PC chassis you can buy on Newegg right now. But that's mostly because Newegg's marketplace is an odd place to be and there are a ton of Hatsune Miku Asus cases on there with four-figure price tags, and I can't figure out why. There's also a $1,000 Asus ProArt chassis on there, but you can also just buy that for $300 direct from Newegg if you'd rather. Which is a roundabout way of me saying that it is pretty much the most expensive chassis you can buy on Newegg without delving into the murky realms of the marketplace.

And, personally, I find it hard to reconcile any notions of value against the MSI Maestro 900R beyond the sheer mass of the thing. Were we going by size and weight, then, I guess it's a match for the Asus ProArt PA602. That's half the weight and half the price, so on a purely per-gram metric, it's all evens Antoine Griezmanns.

But in real terms, it's a massive, expensive case, that I struggle to find genuine ways to justify its cost. There are some neat features, such as that mobo tray, but also some genuine points of frustration that would have me not actually wanting to clothe my PC parts in its black, gold, and glass surrounds. I'm happy with my—what seems to be rather diminutive now—Hyte Y70 Touch. Again, it's half the price, but at least I can get at my PC bits and not break my spine picking it up off the ground.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close, there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

Dave has been gaming since the days of Zaxxon and Lady Bug on the Colecovision, and code books for the Commodore Vic 20 (Death Race 2000!). He built his first gaming PC at the tender age of 16, and finally finished bug-fixing the Cyrix-based system around a year later. When he dropped it out of the window. He first started writing for Official PlayStation Magazine and Xbox World many decades ago, then moved onto PC Format full-time, then PC Gamer, TechRadar, and T3 among others. Now he's back, writing about the nightmarish graphics card market, CPUs with more cores than sense, gaming laptops hotter than the sun, and SSDs more capacious than a Cybertruck.

#4048. It sounds like you shouldn't expect Destiny 2's campaign unvaulting to be ready until 2028, as Bungie tease their plans for the future of the series

When Bungie announced that they would be ceasing to work on major updates for Destiny 2 earlier this year, it obviously felt like that was the end of that, and any future games were not guaranteed whatsoever. Then last month, they announced that they'll be bringing back all of the shooter's vaulted campaigns, which is obviously a lot of work! Now, in a blog post, the developer has outlined where they're at with this process, offering up a timeline of when to expect the unvaulted campaigns, what will be included with them, and light teases for whatever comes after that.

"Our first pass for unvaulting, available to all players, focuses on getting our campaign slate whole again," head of product Josh Deane explains in the blog post. "We're specifically targeting the activity content of Campaigns, Strikes, and Raids from vaulted expansions. Menagerie holds a special place in our hearts (and we've seen years of community requests for a return), so it will be a part of this pass as well." In practical terms, that means the return of the Red War, Forsaken, Curse of Osiris and Warmind campaigns, strikes, raids and raid lairs from said campaigns, and Menagerie Activity with reprised rewards.

The process for this unvaulting apparently began in June as the team scoped the feasibility of it all, and as of now it's pre-production. Full-on production is expected to start in February 2027 at the latest, but it's worth noting that this is expected to take about 12 months to wrap up. That means you won't be jumping back into any of these beloved expansions until 2028 at least, by the sounds of things.

The team also has "stretch goals" that they're investigating for either the unvaulting launch or sometime after, specifically for things like free roam destinations, seasonal activities from Sundial (season 9) to The Coil (season 32), raid and raid lair weapon updates, and PvP maps.

There are seemingly bigger plans for the game too, with some kind of "celebration" to come beyond Moment of Triumph with "new updates", and something referred to as Destiny 'Legacy'; "Our epic journey started over a decade ago, and the whole experience needs to be served to you all where you play today. Expect more information when we come back to you all early next year." Certainly sounds like they're talking about the original Destiny here, but I suppose we should take that with a pinch of salt. Lastly, they mention "Redacted," which is accompanied by this line, "Launch Ventrilo Message: 'We’re back'". No idea what that means, I'll leave that to you Destiny-heads.

Essentially, the core message seems to be that Bungie are "building a new future for Destiny," so, it's not totally dead in the water. You can expect the next major comms update from Bungie in February, too.

#4047. Marathon To Add New Co-Op Roguelite Mode, Social Spaces, And Other Major Features In December

It's beginning to look a lot like Destiny

Bungie isn't prepared to let its extraction shooter go quietly. Instead, Marathon's upcoming 'Symbiosis' update arrives on December 8, bringing a whole host of new PvE and PvP modes. Having just finished watching the new gameplay trailer above, I've got to say, It's giving off plenty of Destiny vibes.

I'm a big, big fan of Marathon, but that's not to say I don't think the game needs a shake-up. It clearly needs something to keep things ticking along. I can't help but feel extremely hyped now that Bungie has shared a first look at all the new content coming next month.

The most interesting addition of the bunch is 'Limbo': a new social space. This is where runners can hang out, chat, test weapons at the firing range and challenge each other in the duelling pit. It reminds me of The Tower from Destiny 2.

Social spaces play a huge role in fostering a sense of community in games, and Bungie knows all about that. Just look at the time Destiny players gathered at The Tower en masse to mourn the passing of Lance Reddick, the voice of Commander Zavala.

Beyond that, 'Expedition' is a new co-op PvE roguelite mode. No PvP, just you and your crew going against new threats. PlayStation.Blog shared an official description of the the new mode:

"Expedition: Phase 1 of a new PvE-only mode built around a three-run series. Play solo or with a crew, face new combat and environmental challenges without PvP threats, and use Flash Boosts to shape your build during a run."

If battling it out against other runners is more your style, Marathon is getting it's first PvP mode, Deathmatch (Beta) pitting quick 3v3 matches against one another. Personally, I think this is a great way to let players get used to the game's arsenal of weapons and gadgets without the time commitment that comes with extraction.

There are a few other new bits and bobs coming to Marathon in December, including a new runner shell, which we'll cover below:

To coincide with the Symbiosis update, Bungie will also be hosting an Open Play Week starting December 8, allowing new players to download and play Marathon for free.

#4046. After the rough start that was last year's entry, Football Manager 27 is looking to bring you in with a few free days of play before the game's even out

Football Manager 27 is still a good week and ahead out from launch, but if you're quick you can already get to playing it. That's because developer Sports Interactive have released a Launch Preview version of the game that lets you take it for a kickabout before it comes out in earnest.

As the devs explain in a Steam blog post, "running for the next five days, the FM27 Launch Preview will be freely playable," across all of its release platforms. "There’s no additional sign-up required, simply download from your preferred platform and begin turning your football vision into dugout decisions. This is your chance to get hands-on with the complete FM27 experience across all game modes, including Shuffle Draft, the fast-paced new multiplayer addition."

One caveat worth noting is that there may be some bugs or glitches in the game that the devs "will work to address in future updates." This, understandably, may be a touchy subject for some. It didn't exactly have a stellar launch, with early patches having to fix hundreds of bugs and other issues. Not that Steam reviews are the be all, end all, but the game is still sitting at a mostly negative a year on. It's very well possible that getting the new one in folks' hands early is a way to bring back some of the audience they may have lost last year.

Still, it doesn't sound like Football Manager 26 was all bad. Phil spent a lofty 227 hours on the game around when it launched, writing for RPS at the time, "That massive database of players, staff and clubs, layered so expertly over time with systems that make them all feel alive and dynamic, is still thrilling. It’s not a new feature by any stretch, but it feels overly punitive to discount it because the menus are bad and it chugs along whenever you press continue. It’s a bad version of a fundamentally great experience, and that means my brain’s going to be full of AS Roma matters for the foreseeable, no matter how many AI gravestones I see in my feed decrying the death of the series."

#4045. Beloved Co-Op Adventure Big Walk in Hot Water After Failing to Disclose AI Usage

Big Walk, one of the most highly-rated games of 2026, has suddenly found itself in a spot of bother, and it's all thanks to those controversial AI tools.

This story stems from the Independent Games Festival Awards (IGF); some of the jurors have taken a hard stance against usage of generative AI or LLM technology.

These jurors recently put out a statement in which they condemn the tech, and in the aftermath of this, it's come out that developer House House did in fact use gen AI, albeit in a minor capacity, when making Big Walk.

On the game's official website, this is now addressed directly in a new FAQ page.

In the statement, House House says LLMs were used "sparingly" near the end of the game's production "to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs."

"In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

The statement goes on to provide an example of how and why the tech was used.

Ultimately, it seems the team has utilised AI very minimally, but that its use was not previously disclosed has rubbed people the wrong way.

Usually, generative AI usage is declared on a game's Steam page, but House House says it didn't do so because "the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage" but has made it public information in light of IGF's actions.

It opens up the debate about gen AI once again. Whether you like it or not, more and more games are being built with the tech to varying degrees, and I expect the number will only grow bigger over time.

However, its ubiquity doesn't safeguard it from criticism, especially when it comes to generating in-game assets, writing, or other creative aspects.

In Big Walk's case, an LLM was used to help with specific technical issues, which I think is relatively harmless, but others may still feel any gen AI is too much.

"Creating new and unique products is our top priority"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Nintendo exec has stressed the importance of creating the company's signature experiences with the rise of AI development.

During a recent investors' meeting attended by multiple Nintendo employees, a question was asked about the company's emphasis on game quality, noting that this, in turn, "seems to be lengthening the development period for each title." The question then poses how Nintendo plans to balance creativity with business management.

Yusuke Beppu, senior executive officer and corporate director for Nintendo, responds, "Development is the engine of Nintendo's competitiveness and value. Creating new and unique products is our top priority," adding that "balancing creativity and business is always challenging." Beppu continues, "Unless we satisfy consumers, our efforts will not lead us to good business results."

Beppu goes on to say that "technologies like the internet and AI have dramatically increased the amount of digital content available to the world," noting the sheer amount of free entertainment available. He also says "we are conducting business in an environment that is different from the past," and that given this increased competition, "it is important to offer unique entertainment experiences that are very Nintendo, so that consumers will choose Nintendo."

With the question itself about Nintendo's lengthy development periods, it's worth noting that Nintendo has been releasing games pretty much every month since the Nintendo Switch 2 launched, sometimes multiple, compared to the likes of Sony and Xbox; I'd say that's pretty fast. With or without AI.
